title: SRE standards: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, and runbooks
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines Redwood Inference’s SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning practices, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and runbook structure. The goal is to provide a consistent, auditable approach that teams can adopt to improve availability, predictability, and operational maturity.

Scope: Applies to all customer-facing inference services (hosted API endpoints, model-serving runtime, routing layer, and telemetry pipelines) and infra components that impact customer-facing SLOs.

Owners and escalation contacts

- Primary owner: eng-sre team (oncall rotation: #eng-sre-oncall)
- Service owners: listed in each service’s SLO page (e.g., Redwood-API, Inference-Router, KV-Cache, Telemetry-Pipeline)
- Pager rotation: follow the oncall schedule in /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-and-incident-response

1) SLO definitions and examples

Principles:
- SLOs must be customer-centric and measurable (availability, latency/percentiles, correctness)
- Keep SLO surface small: 1–3 SLOs per product area (e.g., availability + 95th latency)
- Use rolling windows for reporting (30d rolling window default; 7d window allowed for canaries)
- Define the error budget, burn policies, and automated actions tied to burn rate thresholds

Mandatory metadata for an SLO page:
- SLO name, metric, measurement source (Prometheus/CloudWatch/Datadog), aggregation method, window (30d default), target, error budget, owner, alerting rules, and rollback/mitigation playbooks.

Example: Redwood-API - Generation Path
- Metric: successful_request_ratio (generation success, excluding client errors)
- Measurement: Prometheus rule redwood.api.generation_success_ratio (aggregated, rolling 30d)
- Target: 99.95% availability over 30d
- Error budget: 0.05% -> ~21.6 minutes of downtime per 30d window
- Latency SLO (secondary): p95_response_time < 120ms over 30d
- Owner: product-service-team (service-owner@redwood.ai)
- Alerts: Pager alert on error_budget_burn_rate > 2x sustained for 15 minutes; Slack notification on any breach

2) Error budget policy and automated actions

Error budget states and actions:
- Normal (burn <= 1x expected): standard oncall procedures
- Elevated (burn between 1x and 3x over a 1h window): require service owner involvement and post-incident triage within 48h
- Critical (burn > 3x over a 30m window OR total remaining budget < 10%): paused feature rollouts, freeze non-essential deploys, escalate to Eng+Product leadership, and open a reliability initiative ticket (RI)

Burn rate calculator guidance: teams must publish a short README and a Prometheus query used to compute burn rate. Example query snippet (PromQL):
- "(1 - sum(rate(redwood_api_errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(redwood_api_requests_total[5m])))" // used as part of success_ratio computation

3) Capacity planning and headroom targets

Principles:
- Plan for steady-state traffic + 2.5x traffic spike headroom for 95th percentile traffic patterns for hosted APIs; for Dedicated pools, size to customer commit with 30% burst headroom
- Use capacity models driven by historical qps, token/sec per request, model memory/KV cache state, and expected variance during release/marketing events

Capacity runbook outline:
1. Collect baseline metrics (qps, avg tokens/request, p95 latency, GPU utilization, memory/KV hit rate) for the last 90 days
2. Define growth assumptions (monthly active usage growth, marketing event multipliers)
3. Determine required GPU count and instance types using per-model perf profiles from eng-serving-runtime
4. Plan for autoscale and pre-warm thresholds; configure burst lanes for Dedicated customers
5. Validate in staging: run soak tests at target load and 2x load for 4 hours

Headroom targets (examples):
- Hosted API: baseline + 2.5x spike capacity for p95 load
- Dedicated (reserved pools): baseline commit + 30% burst reserve
- Private/on-prem: align with customer SLA; recommend +25% compute reserve for upgrades and maintenance windows

4) Reliability initiatives (RIs) and investment taxonomy

RI types:
- Incident Remediation (short-term fixes to prevent repeat incidents)
- Architectural (long-term changes: autoscaler redesign, multi-region routing)
- Observability (new metrics, dashboards, tracing)
- Cost/Performance (batching, quantization changes)

RI requirements:
- Every RI must include: problem statement, acceptance criteria tied to SLOs/error budget, owners, timeline, rollout plan, verification tests, rollback plan, and estimated cost (engineering hours + infra)
- Prioritization: align RIs with error budget impact and customer exposure. A critical error budget breach should create a mandatory RI within 7 days.

5) Incident review and postmortem standards

Incident roles:
- Incident Commander (IC): leads triage and communication
- Scribe: documents timeline and actions in the incident doc
- SME(s): responsible engineers for affected services
- Communications lead: coordinates external/customer comms

Postmortem requirements (blameless):
- Timeline of events (UTC timestamps), detection method, impact quantification (customers affected, error budget consumed, revenue-impact estimate if applicable), root cause analysis using 5 Whys or causal graphs, mitigating and preventive action items (with owners and due dates), and link to runbook changes or code PRs.
- All Sev1/Sev2 incidents must have a published postmortem within 7 calendar days. Sev3+ incidents should have postmortems at the discretion of the IC if there is repeat impact or customer complaints.
- Postmortem labels: severity, services affected, CI/CD change ids, release tags.

6) Runbook standards and template

Runbook must be concise and actionable. Minimum sections:
- Title & Scope
- Owner & Oncall rotation
- Symptoms & detection (metric names and thresholds)
- Impact assessment (what to check first)
- Immediate mitigation steps (ordered list of shell/CLI commands and expected outputs)
- Recovery validation checks (queries/devices to run)
- Post-incident actions and links to postmortem template

Example runbook excerpt for "Inference-Router: High 5xx rate":
- Symptom: sustained 5xx rate > 0.5% for 10 minutes (promql: increase(redwood_api_5xx_total[10m]) / increase(redwood_api_requests_total[10m]) > 0.005)
- Owner: inference-routing-team, pager: @inference-route-oncall
- Immediate checks:
  1) Check service health on k8s: kubectl -n inference get pods -l app=inference-router -o wide
  2) Check recent deploys: git log --since="24 hours" --pretty=oneline -- <deploy-manifest> or check CI/CD deploy dashboard
  3) Check memory/GPU pressure: kubectl top pods -n inference | grep inference-router
  4) Tail logs for errors: kubectl -n inference logs -l app=inference-router --since=10m | grep -i error
- Mitigations (ordered):
  - If CPU/GPU saturation: scale replicas up by +2 replicas: kubectl scale deploy inference-router --replicas=<current+2> -n inference
  - If a recent config/deploy is suspect: rollback to previous replicaSet: kubectl rollout undo deploy/inference-router -n inference
  - If dependent service (KV cache) is failing: switch routing policy to cache-bypass using admin CLI: redwood-admin routing set-policy inference-router --policy bypass-cache
- Recovery validation: run synthetic generation /healthcheck endpoint and validate p95 latency < 120ms for 5 consecutive minutes and 0 5xx observed

7) Operational tooling and observability baseline

Required tooling:
- Metrics: Prometheus (service metrics), Datadog (aggregations and business dashboards)
- Tracing: Jaeger/OpenTelemetry for request traces across router -> runtime -> model backends
- Logging: structured logs in JSON via EFK stack; link logs to traces via request_id header
- Alerting: PagerDuty for pagers, Slack for walled garden notifications, email for leadership alerts
- CI/CD: Canary deploy integration with SLO checks (automatic pause if canary consumes >25% of error budget over 1h)

Dashboards and alerts baseline:
- Per-service SLO dashboard: current window compliance, burn rate graph, top error types, owner contact
- Capacity dashboard: GPU utilization, queue depth, pending requests, token/sec, autoscaler behavior
- Oncall runbook widget: link to runbook and recent incidents for service

8) Governance, review cadence, and training

- SLO and runbook review: quarterly review for high-customer-impact services; annual review for internal infra
- Error budget review meeting: weekly cross-functional review where any service with remaining budget < 50% in current window must present mitigation plan
- Runbook drills: quarterly game-days to validate critical runbooks with simulated incidents; require at least 2 runbook exercise participants from the service team
- New hire SRE training: include SLO fundamentals, runbook usage, PromQL examples, PagerDuty run-through
